claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy is single-phase and has homogeneous grain and grain-boundary chemistry.
The initial alloy has no detectable grain-boundary segregation or secondary phases.
Prolonged thermal cycling and cyclic mechanical loading induce localized decomposition in the alloy.
The localized decomposition produces nanoscale elemental segregation, clusters, or brittle precipitates at or near grain boundaries.
Service-induced grain-boundary decomposition develops slowly rather than through immediate impurity-driven segregation.
Conventional alloys exhibit immediate impurity-driven grain-boundary failure relative to the proposed high-entropy-alloy behavior.
High-entropy alloys inherently exhibit sluggish diffusion.
Under cyclic thermal-mechanical loading, sluggish diffusion eventually permits local chemical inhomogeneities to develop.
Local chemical inhomogeneities nucleate nanoprecipitates or clusters at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary nanoprecipitates or clusters act as stress concentrators.
The grain-boundary stress concentrators initiate brittle fracture and degrade toughness.
Thermally and mechanically cycled samples will have lower fracture toughness than the uncycled homogeneous baseline.
Thermally and mechanically cycled samples will exhibit more intergranular fracture features than the baseline.
Thermally and mechanically cycled samples will contain detectable nanoscale grain-boundary precipitates or segregation.
The baseline as-cast alloy has high toughness.
The proposed embrittlement becomes significant only after a threshold exposure time or number of cycles.
Two sample sets from the same as-cast batch, one exposed to combined thermal cycling and fatigue and one retained as an uncycled control, provide the controlled comparison.
HRTEM and APT can be used to assess nanoscale segregation or precipitate formation at grain boundaries.
Fracture-toughness testing can determine whether loading causes a statistically significant toughness reduction relative to the control.
The absence of both a statistically significant toughness reduction and detectable grain-boundary clustering or precipitates after exposure would falsify the hypothesis.
